questions.q: How many profiles can a single Salesforce user have?
options: As many as needed, stacked together
Exactly one, assigned at user creation and required
Zero or one, at the admin's discretion
Exactly one per app the user has access to
questions.explain: Every user has exactly one profile, assigned when the user record is created, and it's required.

questions.q: Besides object CRUD, which of these does a profile also control, per this lesson?
options: Login hours, IP ranges, and password policy
The organization-wide default for every object
The company's Stripe billing settings
Which records a user owns
questions.explain: The lesson lists login hours, login IP ranges, and password policy among the settings only profiles control, not permission sets.

questions.q: What's the key difference between standard and custom profiles today?
options: Standard profiles grant more access than custom ones in every org
Custom profiles can only be used for System Administrator
Standard profiles' CRUD on standard objects is locked since Winter '21; custom profiles remain fully editable
There is no difference -- the terms are interchangeable
questions.explain: The lesson explains editing standard objects on standard profiles has been disabled since Winter '21, while custom profiles stay editable.

questions.q: What does Salesforce's own help documentation recommend for managing object permissions, per this lesson?
options: Build a unique profile for every individual user
Use permission sets and permission set groups instead of profiles where possible
Avoid permission sets entirely and rely only on profiles
Manage all object permissions through the role hierarchy
questions.explain: The lesson quotes Salesforce's guidance to use permission sets and permission set groups over profiles to avoid profile proliferation.

questions.q: A team needs identical object/field access but one user needs a different password expiration policy. Can a permission set alone solve this?
options: Yes, permission sets fully control password policy
No -- password policy is set on the profile, not permission sets, so the policy difference requires a different profile (or a session policy) for that user
Yes, because permission sets override profile settings entirely
No, because password policy can only be set org-wide with no per-user variation
questions.explain: The guide states password policy is a profile-level setting that permission sets can't touch, so a differing policy needs a different profile (or session-level setting), not a permission set.
